sections.heading: Asking for more than human approval
sections.text: My Lord, please do not let my ministry stop at being liked, respected, or praised by people. Do something deeper than that. Work real grace in the hearts of those who hear. Bring to yourself everyone you have chosen and are calling. Strengthen and build up those who already belong to you, and put lasting blessing on their souls.
theological_themes: Ministry must aim at God’s saving and strengthening work, not human applause.
Only God can awaken faith, call sinners, and build up his people through the ministry of the Word.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes ministry as something entrusted by God and carried out to please him rather than to seek praise from people. This directly grounds the prayer’s desire for faithfulness over reputation.
Paul endures ministry hardship for the sake of those God will save in Christ. This supports the prayer’s concern that God would call his people and bring them to salvation through gospel ministry.

sections.heading: Keeping me from making ministry about myself
sections.text: Save me from thinking too highly of myself. Save me from using your work to build my own name, feed my ego, or get something for myself. Let me be glad to be small if Christ is seen as great.
theological_themes: Humility is necessary for faithful ministry.
The minister is not the point; Christ is the message and the treasure.

scripture_references.connection: Paul says that gospel ministry proclaims Christ as Lord and the minister as a servant for Jesus’ sake. That frames the prayer’s rejection of self-promotion in ministry.
John the Baptist’s posture of decreasing while Christ increases captures the prayer’s desire to be humbled so that Christ is exalted.

sections.heading: Making weak words fruitful by your power
sections.text: Please water the hearts of the people who hear your Word. I know the seed is often sown through my weakness, with imperfect words and mixed motives, but you can raise it up with power. Let both me and my hearers see you now by true faith, and one day see you in the brightness of your glory.
theological_themes: God gives growth to the Word that is preached.
Faith sees Christ truly now, while future glory will bring fuller sight.
Human weakness does not prevent God’s power from bearing fruit.

scripture_references.connection: Paul distinguishes between human planting and watering and God’s act of giving growth. This supports the prayer’s dependence on God to make preaching fruitful.

Paul connects the knowledge of God’s glory in Christ with treasure carried in fragile vessels. This illuminates the prayer’s hope that weak ministry can still display divine power and lead people to behold God.

sections.heading: Letting the gospel work in me too
sections.text: Do not let me preach grace as if I do not need it myself. Make every sermon a means of grace to me as well. Let me know, not just explain, the power of your dying love. Let the blood of Christ be medicine for my soul, your nearness my joy, your smile a taste of heaven, and the cross the place where I see both your truth and your mercy clearly.
theological_themes: The minister must personally live from the gospel he proclaims.
Christ’s death is the source of cleansing, healing, mercy, and joy before God.
The cross reveals God’s justice and mercy together.

scripture_references.connection: Paul tells Timothy to pay close attention both to himself and to his teaching. This supports the prayer’s request that preaching would affect the minister’s own soul, not only the hearers.
Paul presents Christ’s blood as the place where God shows both righteousness and mercy toward sinners. This grounds the prayer’s language about the cross as the meeting place of truth and mercy.
Paul’s only boast is the cross of Christ, which fits the prayer’s desire to experience and treasure Christ’s dying love personally.

sections.heading: Confessing my weakness and asking you to stay with your people
sections.text: Lord, you see the doubts and discouragements that come with this calling. Keep me from acting important because of it. Forgive my many sins, the good I have left undone, and all my weakness—both as a man and as a minister. Please bless my poor and unworthy labor, and bless the message of salvation you have given me to speak. Stay with your people. Let your presence be their portion, and mine too.
theological_themes: Ministers remain sinners who need forgiveness and mercy.
God’s grace is needed to make weak labor useful.
God’s presence is the true portion of his people.

scripture_references.connection: John teaches believers to confess sin to God and receive forgiveness and cleansing. This supports the prayer’s honest confession of sins, omissions, and weaknesses.
Christ’s power is shown in human weakness, which grounds the prayer’s request that God bless weak and unworthy labor.
The psalmist finds his deepest portion in God himself. This supports the prayer’s desire that God’s presence would be the lasting inheritance of both minister and people.

sections.heading: Preaching so Christ is exalted and sinners are humbled
sections.text: When I preach to others, do not let my words be only impressive, polished, clever, or well-delivered while lacking spiritual life. Keep me from giving people a performance instead of the truth. Let my preaching lift up Christ and bring sinners low before you in repentance and faith. Lord of power and grace, every heart is in your hands, and every outcome belongs to you. Put the mark of your almighty will on my ministry, and make it serve your purposes.
theological_themes: Preaching must depend on God’s power, not rhetorical skill or performance.
Faithful ministry exalts Christ and calls sinners to humble repentance.
God is sovereign over hearts, events, and the fruit of ministry.

scripture_references.connection: Paul deliberately refuses to ground ministry in impressive speech so that faith rests on God’s power. This directly supports the prayer’s rejection of polished but powerless preaching.
Paul describes proclaiming Christ, warning and teaching everyone, while relying on God’s energy at work in him. This fits the prayer’s desire to exalt Christ and labor under God’s power.
Paul speaks of God working all things according to his will. This grounds the prayer’s final appeal for God’s sovereign purpose to rest on the ministry.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original assumes a Reformed understanding of election and God’s effectual calling; this has been preserved in broad biblical language without trying to resolve denominational differences.

The phrase “means of grace” can carry different ecclesial meanings across traditions. It has been retained in the sense of God using the preached Word to strengthen faith and work grace in the hearer, including the minister.
significant_interpretive_choices: “Special faith” was rendered as true or saving faith in the present, contrasted with the future sight of God in glory.

The original’s images—Christ’s blood as balm, his presence as bliss, his smile as heaven, and the cross as the meeting place of truth and mercy—were kept in contemporary form rather than flattened into abstract theological statements.

“Elegant and masterly” preaching was interpreted as technically impressive but spiritually powerless ministry, so the modern version contrasts performance with Spirit-dependent proclamation of Christ.
